# claudinite-growth

Opt into the **growth lifecycle** — declaring this pack enrolls a repo in contributing its hard-won
lessons up to the shared Claudinite canon, and in pruning its local packs once the canon owns them.
Seeded by default (`--init` + the one-time `grow-with-claudinite-seed` baseline migration for the
existing fleet), and **opt-out by removal**: baselining never re-adds it.

This pack carries the **repo-side** stages of the growth lifecycle: capturing a repo's own
lessons into its local packs, and pruning them once the shared canon covers them. The central
**promote** stage — which lifts portable lessons up into the shared canon — is a home-only duty
that runs canon-side, not a repo-side task, so it lives outside this pack.

Its scheduled work is four tasks under this pack's own `tasks/`, each discovered by the repo's
scheduler (`packs/claudinite-tasks/discover.mjs`) wherever the pack is declared:

| Task | Runs when | Where it lands |
|---|---|---|
| `growth-extract` ([tasks/growth-extract/task.md](tasks/growth-extract/task.md)) | the project changed in the window | the repo's own local packs, via a PR that auto-merges after CI |
| `growth-dedup` ([tasks/growth-dedup/task.md](tasks/growth-dedup/task.md)) | weekly, when the canon or the project's local packs moved in the week | the repo's own local packs, via a PR that auto-merges after CI |
| `prose-to-checks-sweep` ([tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md](tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)) | weekly (no-ops cheaply on a quiet corpus) | a PR converting always-testable pack prose into checks |
| `rule-revalidation` ([tasks/rule-revalidation/task.md](tasks/rule-revalidation/task.md)) | weekly | corrections to rules whose environment claim no longer probes true — auto-merging inside the repo's own local packs, reviewed where they reach a canon pack |

(Plus two agentless tasks over the conversation-logs branch: [usage-fold](../claudinite-tasks/tasks/usage-fold/README.md) hourly,
described below, and `logs-prune` — retention, [tasks/logs-prune/worker.mjs](tasks/logs-prune/worker.mjs).)

## Extraction is one task over two sources

`growth-extract` is the whole capture stage, and it runs **three skills** in order:

1. [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) over the window's commits, merged
   PRs and issue discussion;
2. [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) over the logs captured
   from working sessions;
3. [prose-to-checks](skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md) over the prose **that run just wrote**, to see
   whether any of it upgrades to a check before the PR opens.

Everything lands in **one** PR, delivered to land where the repo's delivery settings allow
(`packs/claudinite-tasks/deliver-pr.md`). The two extraction halves used to be two tasks firing in
the same nightly anchor against the same local packs; they share the lesson bar, the promotion ladder
and the dedup surface ([extracting-lessons.md](extracting-lessons.md)), so the split bought nothing
and cost a second opus dispatch, a second PR, and two runs deduping against a corpus the other was
concurrently writing.

The third step is why the standing `prose-to-checks-sweep` is **weekly**: fresh prose is already
offered a conversion the night it is written, so what the sweep sees is a backlog that moves on a
weekly clock.

A member that wants the local stages without contributing lessons upstream **opts out of
promotion** on its own entry — `{ "id": "claudinite-growth", "config": { "promote": false } }`
— and the central promote stage skips it (absent or `true` = participate).

## The conversation lifecycle — capture in-session, extract in the daily task, retention

The pack also owns **extraction from working sessions**, replacing the old in-session post-merge
lessons pass. Capture and extraction split by what each needs: **capture** needs the live session
transcript, so it runs in-session (at merge, and again when the session ends); **extraction** only
reads the already-pushed logs, so it is the conversation half of the ordinary `growth-extract`
scheduled task — the logs branch is *in the repo*, so reading it, committing lessons to local packs,
and pruning are plain local git on the working tree; only posting the summary on the issue uses the
GitHub MCP tools.

1. **Capture — a step in the merge-to-main skill** (in-session, where the transcript lives).
   Right after a merge lands:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo itself: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`).
   Deterministic, seconds; it bundles the session transcript (sidechains inline, timestamp
   order), **scrubs enumeration-first** (every value the environment holds — `process.env`
   minus a short named allowlist of structural values, plus known credential stores — is
   redacted wherever it appears, with credential-shape patterns as the backstop; a secret the
   session itself transformed is beyond any static scrub, and push protection is the last
   net), and pushes one file per **capture event** onto the orphan **`conversation-logs`**
   branch: `<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`, commits marked `[skip ci]`.
   **Delta-aware, keyed on the session id:** every capture pushes only the entries after this
   session's previous capture, whatever event produced it, so any two events chain into
   disjoint files and a zero delta pushes nothing at all. Double-writing is therefore safe by
   construction, not by coordination — the property [`session-end.mjs`](session-end.mjs) relies
   on, so `test/pack.test.mjs` pins it directly.
   The branch is a **work queue, not an archive** — never merged; tips are cheap in shallow
   session clones and retention keeps them bounded.
1. **Capture — again, when the session ends** ([session-end.mjs](session-end.mjs), invoked by the

--- usage fold fields:
# Usage fold — the repo's own past-data plane

**This task runs no agent.** It is `agent_model: none` with `code-work: node worker.mjs`, so the whole pass is the deterministic [`worker.mjs`](worker.mjs) the executor runs as code-work, which calls its sibling in this folder, the counting and folding core ([`fold-usage.mjs`](fold-usage.mjs)). This file is the human-facing record of what that worker does; there is no agent phase.

## What it does

Daily, when the repo moved: fetch this repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch and count each capture file still inside the retention window; list the scheduler's and the executor's completed workflow runs since the last fold; list the work items that closed since the last fold, and the parks each of them collected; list the pull requests merged since the last fold, with what each took from opening, from its issue and from the session that did the work; deepen and read the local git history and the releases listing; and regenerate `.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json` on a PR that lands itself where this repo's delivery settings allow (the shared landing helper, `packs/claudinite-tasks/land-pr.mjs`, owns those nuances — a `review` repo's PR waits for the owner). A recompute that differs only in its `generated` stamp opens nothing, and a repo with no logs branch yet still folds every other source.

### Why daily, and what stops it being daily noise

This file is the **past-data plane the dashboard renders from** ([claudinite-dashboard](../../../claudinite-dashboard/README.md)): every panel reaching further back than one page of live reads comes from here, so the file's freshness *is* the page's. The cadence is affordable because the sources are — the capture files are local git, and the REST side is a handful of listings, all watermarked, plus one narrow read per item this fold is seeing settle for the first time.

# Delivering a scheduled task's pull request

How an executor subagent delivers the PR its task produced — the AGENT lane of the one
delivery procedure. The CODE lane is `land-pr.mjs` beside this file (Action-side workers
run it); **the two must keep saying the same thing** — a nuance changed in one changes in
the other in the same commit. Your GitHub writes go through the session's MCP tools, and
your pushes ride a credential whose events start workflows normally, so — unlike the code
lane — your PR's checks need no help from you to run.

## The branch and the pull request were chosen for you

**Push to the `Target-branch:` your item carries, and onto the `Target-pr:` where it
carries one.** The executor resolved both from the task's `expected_outcome` before
your session started: `fresh_pr` gave you a new branch and left the task's earlier pull
requests alone; `amend_existing_or_create_new_pr` gave you the branch of the task's
newest open pull request when it had no conflicts, and a fresh one otherwise;
`supersede_existing_pr` gave you a fresh branch and listed the earlier ones under
`Supersedes:`. Where there is a `Target-pr:`, push onto it and open nothing — the pull
request already exists and your push updates it. Where there is none, open your pull
request on that branch. Never mint a branch name, never search for an open pull
request to reuse, and never close an earlier run's pull request yourself: the converge
(`converge-item.mjs`, handed `--pr`) closes what `Supersedes:` names once yours
exists, and a run that delivered nothing leaves them where they were.

## Say which task wrote it

**Every commit you push on a task's behalf carries `Claudinite-Task: <pack>/<task>` on
its own line** — the pack and task id from the work item's first line. When you merge,
put the same line in the squash commit's message too: the merge commit is what lands on
the default branch, and it is the one the signal collectors read.

That trailer is how the scheduler tells the project moving from the machinery running. A
task's own delivery must never count as the repo activity that wakes the next task, and
a title is not a reliable way to say so — every new task's title is a new leak. Yours
says it in the commit.

## The task sets the ceiling; the repo decides the rest

Your task's declared `automerge` is a **ceiling, not a plan** (the legacy
`expected_outcome: 'open-pr'` reads as `fresh_pr` with `nothing`, `'merged-pr'` as
`fresh_pr` with `anything`; `none` and `pr` read as `no_code_changes` and `fresh_pr`).
On a request item the authorization is the item's **`Merge:` field** instead,
read within that ceiling: absent means `nothing`, `if-narrow` means the
`narrow-diff` composite, and any other value is the policy expression itself.
Whichever source it came from:

- **`nothing`** — open the PR and stop. Never arm auto-merge, never merge. Nothing below
  applies to you.
- **`anything`** — the task *may* land its PR. Whether it actually lands unreviewed is
  **this repo's** setting, read in step 1 — never the task's own knowledge. The same task

# Delivering a scheduled task's pull request

How an executor subagent delivers the PR its task produced — the AGENT lane of the one
delivery procedure. The CODE lane is `land-pr.mjs` beside this file (Action-side workers
run it); **the two must keep saying the same thing** — a nuance changed in one changes in
the other in the same commit. Your GitHub writes go through the session's MCP tools, and
your pushes ride a credential whose events start workflows normally, so — unlike the code
lane — your PR's checks need no help from you to run.

## The branch and the pull request were chosen for you

**Push to the `Target-branch:` your item carries, and onto the `Target-pr:` where it
carries one.** The executor resolved both from the task's `expected_outcome` before
your session started: `fresh_pr` gave you a new branch and left the task's earlier pull
requests alone; `amend_existing_or_create_new_pr` gave you the branch of the task's
newest open pull request when it had no conflicts, and a fresh one otherwise;
`supersede_existing_pr` gave you a fresh branch and listed the earlier ones under
`Supersedes:`. Where there is a `Target-pr:`, push onto it and open nothing — the pull
request already exists and your push updates it. Where there is none, open your pull
request on that branch. Never mint a branch name, never search for an open pull
request to reuse, and never close an earlier run's pull request yourself: the converge
(`converge-item.mjs`, handed `--pr`) closes what `Supersedes:` names once yours
exists, and a run that delivered nothing leaves them where they were.

## Say which task wrote it

**Every commit you push on a task's behalf carries `Claudinite-Task: <pack>/<task>` on
its own line** — the pack and task id from the work item's first line. When you merge,
put the same line in the squash commit's message too: the merge commit is what lands on
the default branch, and it is the one the signal collectors read.

That trailer is how the scheduler tells the project moving from the machinery running. A
task's own delivery must never count as the repo activity that wakes the next task, and
a title is not a reliable way to say so — every new task's title is a new leak. Yours
says it in the commit.

## The task sets the ceiling; the repo decides the rest

Your task's declared `automerge` is a **ceiling, not a plan** (the legacy
`expected_outcome: 'open-pr'` reads as `fresh_pr` with `nothing`, `'merged-pr'` as
`fresh_pr` with `anything`; `none` and `pr` read as `no_code_changes` and `fresh_pr`).
On a request item the authorization is the item's **`Merge:` field** instead,
read within that ceiling: absent means `nothing`, `if-narrow` means the
`narrow-diff` composite, and any other value is the policy expression itself.
Whichever source it came from:

- **`nothing`** — open the PR and stop. Never arm auto-merge, never merge. Nothing below
  applies to you.
- **`anything`** — the task *may* land its PR. Whether it actually lands unreviewed is
  **this repo's** setting, read in step 1 — never the task's own knowledge. The same task
  lands itself on one repo and waits for an owner on another, and both are correct.
- **a policy list** (e.g. `['comment-only-changes', 'readme-changes']`, a folder
  scope such as `['under:product-wiki']`, or an intersection of the two,
  `['under:product-wiki && doc-changes']`) — the task may

Comment class: other

I read the task tree, the delivery contract (`packs/claudinite-tasks/deliver-pr.md`, `land-pr.mjs`) and the usage plane before answering.

## What tasks actually exist

**Declared on this repo** (from `.claudinite-settings.json`):

| Pack | Task | Cadence | Lands as |
|---|---|---|---|
| claudinite-growth | `growth-extract` | daily | amend own PR, auto-merges into local packs |
| | `growth-dedup` | weekly | supersede, auto-merges |
| | `prose-to-checks-sweep` | weekly | amend, auto-merges |
| | `rule-revalidation` | weekly | supersede, auto-merges |
| | `logs-prune` | daily | no PR (disabled here) |
| claudinite-canon-curation | `growth-promote` | daily | amend, **`automerge: nothing`** |
| | `growth-discover-packs` | weekly | amend, **`nothing`** |
| | `upstream-watch` | monthly | **`fresh_pr`**, doc-changes only |
| | `pack-version-bump` | daily | commits to main |
| | `pack-version-history` | weekly | amend, auto-merges |
| claudinite-tasks | `task-janitor`, `usage-fold`, `verify-production`, `implement-request` | — | janitor/queue work; usage-fold auto-merges a GENERATED file |
| basics | `ci-performance` (weekly), `improve-comments` (weekly) | | amend; ci-performance is `automerge: anything` |
| claudinite-lifecycle | `update` (disabled here), `adopt-requested-packs` | | converge |

**Exists on the shelf, not declared here:** dashboard (`publish-pages`, `deploy-oauth-exchange`), fleet-sheepdog (`fleet-baseline`, `fleet-roster`, `fleet-pack-seeds`, `fleet-add-missing-packs`), `product-wiki/wiki-growth`, `chrome-extension/store-release`.

So the four you want kept immediate already *are* immediate — they auto-merge into `.claudinite/local/packs`. The PRs that actually queue for you are `growth-promote`, `growth-discover-packs`, `upstream-watch`, `improve-comments`, and whatever `implement-request` delivers.

## The pattern I'd suggest: a **review lane**

Today a PR's identity is *the task's*: `amend_existing_or_create_new_pr` resolves `Target-pr:` to **that task's** newest open PR. The change is to make the target resolvable by a *named lane* several tasks share.

- New optional task field `review_lane: "<name>"` (e.g. `canon-review`). When present, the executor resolves `Target-branch:`/`Target-pr:` from the lane's newest open PR — the lane's branch is `claudinite/lane/<name>` — instead of the task's own. Everything downstream is unchanged: the run still stamps `Claudinite-Task:`, the converge still closes its item.
- A lane's `automerge` is structurally `nothing`. A lane diff is wide by construction, and a policy is a *prediction of the diff's shape* — no honest prediction covers an accumulating lane.
- Each run appends a dated section to the PR body: which task, which item, what it added. The body becomes the lane's running log, so you read increments rather than re-reading the whole diff (GitHub's "changes since your last review" does the rest).
- Each run **merges `main` into the lane** before writing, rather than forking off it — otherwise the lane drifts conflicted and every run silently falls back to a fresh branch.
- The lane needs a ceiling, or it becomes a dumping ground nobody can approve: after N runs or M days without a merge, the run opens a fresh lane PR and labels the old one. Landing the lane resets it — the next run mints a new one.
- Only *additive, independent* work belongs in a lane — prose, doc corrections, generated rows. Anything with a migration shape keeps its own PR, because approving it is one decision and the lane is another.

**Cheaper first step, available today with no engine change:** `upstream-watch` is `fresh_pr`, which files a fresh PR per cycle and buries whatever needed attention — exactly what rule (85) warns about. Flipping it to `amend_existing_or_create_new_pr` gives each human-gated task *one standing, growing PR* immediately. That may be 80% of what you want; the lane is the step beyond it, collapsing several standing PRs into one.

## Do we learn from execution data? No — the data plane exists, nothing reads it back

`claudinite-tasks/usage-fold` already folds, per day, into `.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json`:

- `skillLoads` per skill **with denominators** (sessions where its trigger plausibly applied),
- `checks` per scope — `runs`, `failures`, `errors`, blocking/advisory volume — and **`checkFindings` per rule id**,
- `taskExec` (success/failed/task-gone/invalid), `queue` outcomes, `parks` per task by kind, `taskCost` in tokens.

The only consumers are `claudinite-dashboard` and the fleet aggregator. Nothing turns any of it into a corpus change. Meanwhile `claudinite-canon-curation/RULES.md` already *states* the policy — "measure its blocking-firing rate against what it buys; a check whose firings are dominated by cases where the agent already did the right thing is a demotion candidate" — with no mechanism behind it. That's the real gap your question found: a **`corpus-effectiveness`** task (weekly, repo-side for local packs; a fleet twin for the canon) reading the aggregate over a window and proposing demotions (check → advisory → prose), retirement of skills that never load against a live denominator, and splits for tasks whose `parks` are dominated by one kind. Its output is precisely the kind of change that should land in the review lane rather than as its own PR.

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

I think we should add a new task idiom: PR name (pattern). This will allow tasks to declare the PR names they look to override/append to/create, thus allowing multiple tasks to work on the same PR, and hopefully, possibly totally disband the notion of task "lane"? This can also allow ad-hoc tasks to define the PR name in advance, and allow task handovers (one task creates/amends a PR, the second does a review or follow up work, for example). This disconnects the notion of "every PR merge closes the related Issue", which should be done discerningly. 
Once we have this mechanism (the default task behavior, without this property defined, should continue to work like today, naming the task), we can consider which of the growth tasks which don't automerge can work on the same PR for human approval.

content.text:
I read the task tree and the usage pipeline rather than proposing from memory. Three answers.

## 1. What tasks exist

26 declarations across the shelf. The ones that run **here** (this repo declares `claudinite-lifecycle`, `claudinite-tasks`, `basics`, `git-github`, `claudinite-growth`, `claudinite-canon-curation`, `local/claudinite`, `claude-code-web-users-support`):

| Task | Cadence | Outcome | Automerge |
|---|---|---|---|
| `claudinite-growth/growth-extract` | daily | amend-or-new | local-pack md + checks |
| `claudinite-growth/growth-dedup` | weekly | supersede | `under:.claudinite/local/packs && markdown-trims` |
| `claudinite-growth/prose-to-checks-sweep` | weekly | amend-or-new | local-pack line removals + checks |
| `claudinite-growth/rule-revalidation` | weekly | supersede | `under:.claudinite/local/packs` |
| `claudinite-growth/logs-prune` | daily | no PR | — (disabled here) |
| `claudinite-canon-curation/growth-promote` | daily, fleet | amend-or-new | **nothing** |
| `claudinite-canon-curation/growth-discover-packs` | weekly, fleet | amend-or-new | **nothing** |
| `claudinite-canon-curation/upstream-watch` | monthly | **fresh_pr** | `under:packs && doc-changes` |
| `claudinite-canon-curation/pack-version-bump` | daily | no PR | — |
| `claudinite-canon-curation/pack-version-history` | weekly | amend-or-new | `pack-version-history` |
| `claudinite-tasks/usage-fold` | daily | amend-or-new | generated-file changes |
| `claudinite-tasks/task-janitor`, `verify-production`, `queue/implement-request` | queue machinery | — | — |
| `basics/improve-comments` | weekly | amend-or-new | comment-only + readme |
| `basics/ci-performance` | weekly | amend-or-new | anything |
| `claudinite-lifecycle/update` (disabled here), `adopt-requested-packs` | — | — | — |

Elsewhere on the shelf: `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/{fleet-baseline, fleet-roster, fleet-pack-seeds, fleet-add-missing-packs}`, `claudinite-dashboard/{publish-pages, deploy-oauth-exchange}`, `product-wiki/wiki-growth`, `chrome-extension/store-release`.

So the set you want kept immediate (the four growth tasks) is already immediate and auto-merging. The review load is **three** tasks: `growth-promote`, `growth-discover-packs`, `upstream-watch` — plus whatever `improve-comments` and `ci-performance` leave outside their policies.

## 2. The pattern: a **review lane**

Today `amend_existing_or_create_new_pr` keys on *the task's own* newest open PR. The pattern is to key it on a **lane** instead:

- new optional declaration field `review_lane: "<name>"`; tasks sharing a lane share one branch and one open PR, and the executor resolves `Target-branch:`/`Target-pr:` from the lane rather than the task id. Everything downstream (`deliver-pr.md`, `land-pr.mjs`) is unchanged — they already just push where they're told.
- each run appends **one commit** carrying its own `Claudinite-Task:` trailer, and one dated section to the PR body, so the reviewer reads an accumulating log rather than a merged blob.
- a lane PR is `automerge: nothing` by construction — a check can hold that, since a lane only exists for work no policy covers. That also keeps the auto-merging growth tasks structurally ineligible, which is what you asked for.
- **bounded, or it becomes the same problem wearing a bigger diff**: the lane closes on a ceiling (an age of ~7 days, or N appended commits), after which the next run opens a fresh lane PR. Each append merges base first; a conflicting append takes a fresh lane and supersedes.

One lane covers it here: `canon-curation` over the three human-gated tasks.

**But** the cheaper move first, with zero engine change: `upstream-watch` is the only one still on `fresh_pr`. Flipping it to `amend_existing_or_create_new_pr` gives every human-gated task exactly one standing PR — three review gates, not N. That may be all you need, and the lane is the upgrade if three still feels like three too many. It's also the fallback the lane degrades to.

## 3. Learning from execution data — no, and the data is already sitting there

`usage-fold` builds `.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json` with exactly the inputs such a task needs: `skillLoads` **with denominators**, `checks` per scope (runs/failures/errors/blocking/advisory), `checkFindings` **per rule id**, `taskExec`, `parks` per `pack/task` by kind, `taskCost`, and `queue` outcomes.

Its only consumers are `claudinite-dashboard/{view-repo,view-fleet,usage,fleet-growth}.mjs` and the sheepdog's fleet aggregator. **Nothing reads it back into the corpus.** Meanwhile `packs/claudinite-canon-curation/RULES.md` already states the rule — *"Deciding whether an enforced check still earns its keep — measure its blocking-firing rate against what it buys"* — with no mechanism that measures it. That is a prose rule waiting for its task.

The missing task, repo-side, weekly, reading the aggregate: checks whose findings are dominated by cases the agent got right anyway → demotion candidates; checks with zero runs → dead scope; skills with loads far below their trigger denominator → wrong description, or retire; tasks whose `parks` are dominated by one kind → a split or a precondition fix; rules never cited by any finding → prose-only. It writes proposals into local packs, and its fleet twin in `claudinite-canon-curation` would do the same over the sheepdog's fleet aggregate against canon packs.

I've made no changes and filed nothing — you dismissed the question, so I'm holding here.

> ⚠️ Still open: which consolidation shape to build (standing-PR flip vs. the `review_lane` field), and whether to file the corpus-effectiveness task. Say the word and I'll open the issues.

# Searching for a tool

- **A search that finds nothing** is evidence about your query, not about the environment: vary
  the query before concluding a capability is absent, and try the tool before telling the owner a
  step is theirs.
- **`select:` matches the fully-qualified name only** — `select:mcp__<server>__<tool>`, copied off
  the deferred-tools listing. A short name after `select:` returns "no matching tools" while the
  tool sits in the listing, so reach for it when you have the server, or to load several at once.
- **A bare short name is a keyword query, and resolves** — `get_teams` on its own returns the
  tool. It is the form to use when you know the name but not the server. (1)
- **A server whose whole roster the deferred-tools listing already names** is the one exception: one
  miss there is the answer, so read the roster rather than rephrase the query.

input.title: A task declares the pull request it works on, by name — so several tasks can share one
input.body:
## The problem

The executor's target seam (`packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/target.mjs`) keys a task's pull requests on the task's own identity — the branch family `claudinite/<pack>/<task>/`, plus the `Claudinite-Task:` trailer on the head commit as the second recogniser. One task, one family, one standing pull request, by construction.

That makes every human-gated task its own review gate. On this repo `growth-promote` (daily), `growth-discover-packs` (weekly) and `upstream-watch` (monthly) all target `packs/`, all declare `automerge: "nothing"`, and all arrive as separate pull requests asking for the same kind of attention. There is no way for a task to say "append to the pull request that already exists", and no way for one task to hand work to another through a pull request.

## The requirement

A task declares **the name of the pull request it works on**. The name is the identity the target seam resolves against, in place of the task id. Tasks declaring the same name share one branch family and therefore one standing pull request; a run appends its commit to whatever is open under that name.

- `pr_name` is optional. **Absent, nothing changes**: the family is `<pack>/<task>` exactly as today, and every existing declaration behaves identically.
- The name is a **pattern**, expanded at resolve time over a closed placeholder vocabulary — `{pack}`, `{task}`, `{date}`, `{week}`, `{month}`. `{month}` is how a shared pull request stays reviewable: the family rotates, so the accumulation is bounded by the calendar rather than growing without end.
- An ad-hoc / `request` task can therefore state the pull request it will land on *before* it runs, and a second task can declare the same name to review or follow up on what the first delivered.

This subsumes the "review lane" grouping: the name is the lane, declared as data on the tasks that share it rather than as a separate concept.

## What it does NOT change

- **Convergence stays per item.** A queue item's own issue is never closed by its pull request merging — `converge-item.mjs` closes or parks it, and an `approval` park stamps `Ends-when: #<pr> closed`, which the janitor's rule G resolves per item. Several items parked on one shared pull request each carry their own `Ends-when:` pointing at it and each close independently when it resolves. Nothing here needs new convergence machinery; the "one PR merge closes one issue" coupling the shared name would break is a coupling the queue never had.
- **`Claudinite-Task:` stays per commit.** Each run stamps its own, so the movement signals keep telling the project moving from the machinery running. Only the *pull request's* identity becomes shared.

## Two constraints this creates

1. **Sharing is only legal for `automerge: "nothing"`.** A shared pull request carries commits from several tasks; landing it on one contributor's policy would land another's work unreviewed. Validated at the door.
2. **The shared name is the mutex.** Two items resolving to the same name must serialise rather than race, keyed on the target the write lands on — never on the item's title.

## Scope of this change

- `pr_name` in `task.schema.json` and `task-contract.mjs` (shape, placeholder vocabulary, expansion, the `automerge` constraint).
- `target.mjs` keyed on the resolved family, with the trailer recogniser kept for the default family only.
- `executor.mjs` passing the family through.
- Tests first, then the docs the two delivery lanes share.

Which growth tasks actually share a name is a follow-up decision, taken once the mechanism exists.

lines: +// THE PULL REQUEST A TASK NAMES (#1950). The target seam recognises a task's pull
+// requests by a branch family; `pr_name` is what a task calls that family, so two
+// tasks declaring the same one land on the same standing pull request and a
+// `request` task can state where it will land before it runs. Absent, the family
+// IS the task id — the shape every declaration written before this had, which is
+// why nothing changes by passing through here.
+// A pattern, not a literal: the placeholders below expand at resolve time, and
+// `{month}` is the one that matters — a shared pull request that never rotates
+// grows until nobody can review it, so the calendar bounds what a ceiling would
+// otherwise have to.
+export const PR_NAME_PLACEHOLDERS = Object.freeze(['pack', 'task', 'date', 'week', 'month']);
+// A family is path-shaped, because it becomes one: `claudinite/<family>/<leaf>`.
+// Segments carry no traversal and no whitespace — a name is a branch prefix before
+// it is anything else.
+const PR_NAME_SEGMENT = /^(?:[A-Za-z0-9._-]+|\{[a-z]+\})+$/;
+// ISO 8601 week, which is the only one of the three stamps that is not a substring
+// of the date: Thursday decides the year a week belongs to.
+function isoWeek(date) {
+  const d = new Date(Date.UTC(date.getUTCFullYear(), date.getUTCMonth(), date.getUTCDate()));
+  d.setUTCDate(d.getUTCDate() + 4 - (d.getUTCDay() || 7));
+  const yearStart = Date.UTC(d.getUTCFullYear(), 0, 1);
+  const week = Math.ceil(((d - yearStart) / 86400000 + 1) / 7);
+  return `${d.getUTCFullYear()}-W${String(week).padStart(2, '0')}`;
+// The family this run works under. `taskId` is `<pack>/<task>`, and an undeclared
+// name resolves to it unchanged.
+export function expandPrName(prName, { taskId, now = Date.now() } = {}) {
+  if (prName === undefined || prName === null || String(prName).trim() === '') return taskId;
+  const at = new Date(now);
+  const iso = at.toISOString();
+  const [pack, ...rest] = String(taskId).split('/');
+  const values = {
+    pack, task: rest.join('/'), date: iso.slice(0, 10), month: iso.slice(0, 7), week: isoWeek(at),
+  return String(prName).replace(/\{([a-z]+)\}/g, (whole, key) => (values[key] === undefined ? whole : values[key]));

+// SHOULD share a pull request is the declarations' own business, and the one thing
+// validated across them (a policy that would land a sibling's work unreviewed) is
+// checked beside `automerge` below.

+  if (typeof prName !== 'string' || prName.trim() === '') return 'it is not a non-empty string';
+  if (prName !== prName.trim()) return 'it is padded with whitespace';
+  const segments = prName.split('/');
+  if (segments.some((s) => s === '')) return 'it has an empty path segment';
+  if (segments.some((s) => s === '.' || s === '..')) return 'it traverses the branch namespace';
+  if (!segments.every((s) => PR_NAME_SEGMENT.test(s))) return 'a segment is not letters, digits, ".", "_", "-" or a {placeholder}';

git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF' && git push -u origin claude/dazzling-shannon-2l5fwg -q && echo pushed
A task names the pull request it works on

The executor's target seam keyed a task's pull requests on the task's own
identity, so one task meant one standing pull request and every human-gated
task was its own review gate. `pr_name` names the branch family instead: two
tasks declaring one name share one pull request, and a request task can state
where it will land before it runs, which is what lets one task hand a pull
request to another.

Absent, the family is the task's own `<pack>/<task>` — every declaration
written before the field behaves exactly as it did.

The name is a pattern over {pack}, {task}, {date}, {week} and {month},
expanded when the run resolves its target; {month} is what keeps a shared
pull request reviewable, rotating the family on the calendar rather than
leaving it to grow without end.

A named pull request carries other tasks' commits, so a task declaring one
may merge nothing and may not supersede — landing it would land a sibling's
work unreviewed, superseding would close a sibling's pull request. The
`Claudinite-Task:` trailer stays per commit and keeps answering which task
wrote what; the trailer recogniser is offered only for the default family,
since on a shared pull request it names whichever task pushed last.

Convergence is untouched: a queue item's issue is closed by converge-item,
never by its pull request merging, and several items parked on one shared
pull request each carry their own `Ends-when:` pointing at it.

Refs #1950

---
name: committing
description: How a commit is cut — one concern per commit, the issue it references, a landed commit revised only by a new one, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
metadata:
  force-load-on-tool-calls:
    - 'Bash.command /(^|[;&|]\s*|\n\s*)git\s+commit\b/'
---

# Committing

- **One concern per commit.** If two changes could each stand alone, split them; a message that
  wants numbered items is the split talking.
- **Reference the issue** — `Refs #n`, or `Fixes #n` / `Closes #n` where the commit finishes it;
  the `task-lifecycle` check reads it off the branch.
- **A landed commit is revised by a new commit**, never a rewrite of that one.
- **Stage by name** — `git add <paths>` for the files this commit is about; `-a` sweeps in whatever
  else was in progress.

input.body:
Closes #1950

The executor's target seam keyed a task's pull requests on the task's own identity — the branch family `claudinite/<pack>/<task>/`, plus the `Claudinite-Task:` trailer as a second recogniser. One task, one standing pull request, by construction, so every human-gated task was its own review gate and no task could hand a pull request to another.

A task now **names** the family: `pr_name`. Two tasks declaring one name share one standing pull request, each run appending its own commit; a `request` task can state the name before it runs.

- **Absent, nothing changes.** The family is the task's own `<pack>/<task>`, so every declaration written before the field resolves exactly as it did.
- **A pattern**, over `{pack}`, `{task}`, `{date}`, `{week}`, `{month}`, expanded when the run resolves its target. `{month}` is what keeps a shared pull request reviewable — the family rotates on the calendar instead of accumulating without end.
- **A named pull request may merge nothing and may not supersede.** It carries other tasks' commits: landing it would land a sibling's work unreviewed, superseding would close a sibling's pull request. Both validated at the door.
- **The trailer recogniser is offered only for the default family.** It answers which *task* wrote a pull request, which on a shared one is whichever pushed last — not the question being asked. A shared family is settled by the branch prefix alone, and reads no head commits.

Convergence is untouched, and did not need to change: a queue item's issue is closed by `converge-item.mjs`, never by its pull request merging, and an `approval` park stamps `Ends-when: #<pr> closed` that janitor rule G resolves per item — so several items parked on one shared pull request each close independently.

Which growth tasks actually share a name is the follow-up decision, taken now that the mechanism exists.

Full suite green: 3444 pass, 0 fail. `check_the_world` reports 0 blocking.

[#1951](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1951) is open, closing [#1950](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1950).

```
packs/claudinite-tasks/
  the pr_name field itself — expandPrName over {pack} {task} {date} {week}
  {month}, prNameProblem for shape, and the two cross-field rules in
  validateTaskDeclaration (a named PR merges nothing, never supersedes);
  the schema entry; deliver-pr.md tells the agent lane a named PR carries
  other tasks' commits and is never landed

packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/
  target.mjs re-keyed from the task id to the family it resolves, with the
  Claudinite-Task trailer recogniser offered only for the default family;
  executor.mjs expands the declared name at the target seam

packs/claudinite-tasks/docs/
  PRINCIPLES.md — three bullets in Deliver, each citing the tests that pin it
```

Your instinct on the lane was right — it dissolves. The name *is* the lane, declared as data on the tasks that share it, and `{month}` in the pattern does the bounding a lane would have needed an age ceiling for.

Two things I decided rather than ask about, both validated at the door: a task declaring a name may merge **nothing** (its PR carries a sibling's commits, so one contributor's policy would land another's work unreviewed), and may not **supersede** (that would close a sibling's PR). Say the word if either is tighter than you want.

On the issue-closing coupling you flagged: it turned out not to need breaking. The queue never had it — `converge-item.mjs` closes or parks the item, an `approval` park stamps `Ends-when: #<pr> closed`, and the janitor resolves that per item. N items on one shared PR each close independently, already.

Not done: which growth tasks actually take a shared name. `growth-promote`, `growth-discover-packs` and `upstream-watch` all target `packs/` and all already declare `automerge: "nothing"`, so `pr_name: "canon-review/{month}"` fits all three — but `upstream-watch` is `fresh_pr` and would want `amend_existing_or_create_new_pr` to accumulate. That's a one-line-per-task follow-up once this lands.

1	---
2	name: writing-tests
3	description: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
4	metadata:
5	  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
6	    - "**/*.test.*"
7	    - "**/*.spec.*"
8	    - "**/*_test.*"
9	    - "**/test_*.*"
10	    - "**/test/**"
11	    - "**/tests/**"
12	    - "**/__tests__/**"
13	    - "**/spec/**"
14	---
15	
16	# Testing practices
17	
18	A consuming repo's own test *mechanics* — runner, layout, which suites exist — are its own docs'; CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha are [git-github-advanced](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)'s.
19	
20	- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work. If the mutation was **staged** (to make a check that scans `git diff --cached` fire), a bare `git checkout -- <file>` restores from the index — which now holds the mutation — so the "restore" is a no-op; use `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (or `git reset` first).
21	- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
22	- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
23	- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once. (3)
24	- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
25	- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
26	- **Never test that a value is set.** A test that reads a value someone declared — a config or manifest field (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'fresh_pr')`), an exported constant or default object (`assert.deepEqual(DEFAULTS, {…})`), a settings file naming a pack, a workflow's `run:` line, a frontmatter key — and asserts it is the literal it was set to restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. "It exists", "it has the right shape" and "it is one of these" are the same test in a looser coat. Test the **behaviour the value drives** instead: feed the real code the declared value and assert what the code does with it — a task declared `weekly` is planned once across a fourteen-day clock, a check declared over `**/*.mjs` fires on a fixture `.mjs` and stays silent on a `.md`, a default object yields the documented output when nothing overrides it. Where no code reads the value there is nothing to test; if a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test. What *does* earn an assertion on declared data is a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set — proven by running the constraint, not by re-listing the set.
27	- **Testing a task's precondition or declaration** — assert only the pack's own code: a
28	  task-local term's decisions, a worker's behaviour, or a composition it designed; a plain
29	  built-in term or a validated declaration is the scheduler's own mechanism, proved once by its
30	  own suite.
31	- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
32	- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
33	- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (1)
34	- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
35	- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.

For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. If the mutation was **staged** (to make a check that scans `git diff --cached` fire), a bare `git checkout -- <file>` restores from the index — which now holds the mutation — so the "restore" is a no-op; use `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (or `git reset` first).

A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.

A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.

Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once. (3)
- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.

input.title: Two runs resolving one pull-request family must serialise, not race
input.body:
Falls out of #1950 / #1951, which named this constraint and did not implement it.

With a family per task, two runs could never resolve the same target: the family *was* the task, and one task holds one item at a time. `pr_name` removes that guarantee. Two tasks sharing a name can be picked in the same drain, or by two executor runs at once, and both resolve the same family — each reading the incumbent, each planning an amend or, worse, each planning `fresh` against an empty list and opening a second pull request under one name.

The repo's own rule says where the guard goes: key it on **the target the write lands on**, never the requester's phrasing — so the resolved family, not the item title. The `Blocked-by:` lane is what already serialises work items, and readiness is re-derived by the scheduler's hourly pass, so the shape is likely: at pick, an item whose resolved family is already held by a live item blocks behind it rather than racing it.

Open questions for whoever takes it:

- Is the family resolved early enough to block on at pick time? It is resolved by the executor *after* the precondition's go, which may be too late to turn the item around cleanly.
- `{date}`/`{week}`/`{month}` in a pattern mean the family is clock-dependent, so two runs either side of a boundary resolve different families and correctly do not contend — the guard must compare resolved names, never the declared pattern.
- What a blocked-on-family item does when its blocker parks rather than closes.

Until this lands, sharing a name is safe only where the sharing tasks cannot be picked concurrently — which is the case for the canon-review candidates (`growth-promote` daily, `growth-discover-packs` weekly, `upstream-watch` monthly, all on the fleet endpoint or well apart), but is not a property anything enforces.

input.body:
Closes #1950

The executor's target seam keyed a task's pull requests on the task's own identity — the branch family `claudinite/<pack>/<task>/`, plus the `Claudinite-Task:` trailer as a second recogniser. One task, one standing pull request, by construction, so every human-gated task was its own review gate and no task could hand a pull request to another.

A task now **names** the family: `pr_name`. Two tasks declaring one name share one standing pull request, each run appending its own commit; a `request` task can state the name before it runs.

- **Absent, nothing changes.** The family is the task's own `<pack>/<task>`, so every declaration written before the field resolves exactly as it did.
- **A pattern**, over `{pack}`, `{task}`, `{date}`, `{week}`, `{month}`, expanded when the run resolves its target. `{month}` is what keeps a shared pull request reviewable — the family rotates on the calendar instead of accumulating without end.
- **A named pull request may merge nothing and may not supersede.** It carries other tasks' commits: landing it would land a sibling's work unreviewed, superseding would close a sibling's pull request. Both validated at the door.
- **The trailer recogniser is offered only for the default family.** It answers which *task* wrote a pull request, which on a shared one is whichever pushed last — not the question being asked. A shared family is settled by the branch prefix alone, and reads no head commits.

Convergence is untouched, and did not need to change: a queue item's issue is closed by `converge-item.mjs`, never by its pull request merging, and an `approval` park stamps `Ends-when: #<pr> closed` that janitor rule G resolves per item — so several items parked on one shared pull request each close independently.

## Not in this change

**Serialisation — #1952.** A family per task made concurrent resolution of one target impossible; a shared family creates it, and this change adds no guard. The tests say so where the fake GitHub stops being able to answer. Until #1952 lands, sharing a name is safe only where the sharing tasks cannot be picked concurrently — true of the canon-review candidates, enforced by nothing.

Which growth tasks actually share a name is the other follow-up, taken now that the mechanism exists.

Full suite green: 3444 pass, 0 fail. `check_the_world` reports 0 blocking. Every new guard was mutated and watched bite: the placeholder/shape rule, the merge-nothing rule, the never-supersede rule, the shared-family resolution and the trailer recogniser's family comparison.

- **Four new guards had never been seen red** (two written after their implementation). Restored from the index each time; tree verified clean.
- **A gap the skill's "say what it can't catch" rule surfaced**: the fake GitHub answers one caller at a time, so nothing in the suite covers **two runs resolving one family concurrently** — a race a family-per-task made impossible and `pr_name` creates. # Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

Please drop the "learn from execution data" direction for this session.

I think all 4 claudinite-growth tasks are irrelevant for this change - they should all have unique PR names, and they should all automerge "under:.claudinite/local" (and the settings file too?)

Regadring automerge - I don't know where you got that idea that we don't automerge with PR names. These are orthogonal. Moreover - all task properties should be orthogonal (no behavior change in property A based on property B value) unless explicitly mentioned. This should be an engineering rule - when you consider making these sort of interactions - make sure the owner explicitly permits it.

So PRs should try to automerge regardless. They can fail to automerge and stay open.

ALSO - what did you say about the lane closes after 7 days? Why would you make this up? Open PRs are awaiting review, and the fact that more tasks work on them means they are alive, not dead. If the owner wants to close them - they will.

Regarding the PR name - would we call the PR exactly the name in the task as string, or pattern match? I can't think of usage for "pattern" now.

Now that we don't have a "task lane" - please make sure the terminology is purged everywhere. If the PR elements are irrelevant to a piece of documentation - make sure to elimination the "lane" notes, don't just rename it.
Also - if a task that has no PRs is stuck/failed - is there a mechanism to not execute the following run? Because that could still be considered a "lane". If it exists - don't bulk-change the docuemntation. We may need to add preconditions for "previous task failed" vs. "existing PR exists" and they have different implementation  - one based on task name and the other based on PR name.

Take all the feedback in, rebuild your solution, and in the end launch a Fable subagent to review it for consistency, and that no redundant assumptions or restrictions were taken.

- searching-for-a-tool: Finding a harness tool by name — the select form for a deferred tool, and what an empty search means. Use before any ToolSearch, and when a search finds nothing.

- working-with-generated-files: Working with a file a test or tool generates — naming it, changing the generator rather than the file, and resolving its merge conflicts by regenerating. Loaded for any edit of a GENERATED file.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. - writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. message.content:
Please drop the "learn from execution data" direction for this session.

I think all 4 claudinite-growth tasks are irrelevant for this change - they should all have unique PR names, and they should all automerge "under:.claudinite/local" (and the settings file too?)

Regadring automerge - I don't know where you got that idea that we don't automerge with PR names. These are orthogonal. Moreover - all task properties should be orthogonal (no behavior change in property A based on property B value) unless explicitly mentioned. This should be an engineering rule - when you consider making these sort of interactions - make sure the owner explicitly permits it.

So PRs should try to automerge regardless. They can fail to automerge and stay open.

ALSO - what did you say about the lane closes after 7 days? Why would you make this up? Open PRs are awaiting review, and the fact that more tasks work on them means they are alive, not dead. If the owner wants to close them - they will.

Regarding the PR name - would we call the PR exactly the name in the task as string, or pattern match? I can't think of usage for "pattern" now.

Now that we don't have a "task lane" - please make sure the terminology is purged everywhere. If the PR elements are irrelevant to a piece of documentation - make sure to elimination the "lane" notes, don't just rename it.
Also - if a task that has no PRs is stuck/failed - is there a mechanism to not execute the following run? Because that could still be considered a "lane". If it exists - don't bulk-change the docuemntation. We may need to add preconditions for "previous task failed" vs. "existing PR exists" and they have different implementation  - one based on task name and the other based on PR name.

Take all the feedback in, rebuild your solution, and in the end launch a Fable subagent to review it for consistency, and that no redundant assumptions or restrictions were taken.

Taking the corrections in order; the invented restrictions and the invented ceiling both go.

content.content:
1	---
2	name: writing-pack-prose
3	description: How pack prose is written — RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon — brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, and the per-pack references doc. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
4	metadata:
5	  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
6	    - "**/packs/*/RULES.md"
7	    - "**/packs/*/skills/*/SKILL.md"
8	---
9	
10	# Writing pack prose
11	
12	Whether a candidate *qualifies* as a rule at all, and which mechanism carries it, is
13	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)'s call — settle it there before writing.
14	
15	**Start from the foundation:** read the "Write each rule" section of
16	[authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md) first — its
17	principles (concrete enough to verify, motivation stated, what to do rather than what not to,
18	the right altitude, emphasis reserved) bind pack prose too. This skill is the pack-specific
19	layer on top of them, and doesn't restate them.
20	
21	## The ration
22	
23	Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every session in every repo that declares the pack,
24	forever, whether or not it ever applies — so prose is rationed, and the ration is small.
25	
26	- **One sentence per rule, near 40 words**: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence
27	  clause only where the rule cannot be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph
28	  to land has not been understood well enough to be a rule yet.
29	- **An extraction pass adds at most two rules.** If more candidates clear the bar, write the
30	  two strongest and drop the rest — they will recur if they were real.
31	- **Split a rule that carries two situations.** Each situation is its own rule with its own
32	  trigger.
33	- A `SKILL.md` loads only when its activity is under way, so it may carry procedure at length —
34	  but it is still rationed by the same test: every line must change what the reader does.
35	  Method, steps and decision points belong there; anything a session must know *without*
36	  loading it belongs in `RULES.md` or a check, and rationale belongs in the references doc
37	  below.
38	- **Moving a rule out of `RULES.md` into a skill** — only where the skill's
39	  `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` covers *every* moment the rule is needed. A skill whose only
40	  trigger is its description is picked by the model, not the harness, so a rule that must fire at
41	  a moment no file edit predicts stays prose, however activity-shaped it reads. (2)
42	
43	## Shape a rule so it fires
44	
45	- **Keying a rule to its trigger** — open with the act the reader is performing, not the state
46	  of the world the rule applies to. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown"; they notice they
47	  are writing an encoder. A rule keyed to a state never fires, because nothing brings the
48	  reader to it.
49	- **Keying a rule the reader reaches while debugging** — name the symptom that sends them
50	  looking ("A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser"), not the act that caused it. By
51	  the time the rule is wanted the act is over, and the symptom is what they can see.
52	- **Keying a rule that corrects a misconception** — name what the reader wants ("Wanting
53	  `import`/`export` in extension code"), not the wrong move they might make ("Reaching for a
54	  bundler"). Someone who doesn't yet know the move is wrong won't recognise themselves in it.
55	- **Phrasing that trigger** — use the words the reader would use for the situation, and put
56	  them first and in bold, so the rule is findable by scanning the left margin alone.
57	- **Choosing the unit** — one block per situation, not one bullet per rule. A reader arrives
58	  holding a problem, so give them the whole decision in one place rather than a cross-reference
59	  to three neighbouring bullets.
60	- **Splitting a rule that only makes sense after the one above it** — don't. If the subject
61	  needs a "that" pointing back ("Writing that record"), it is a clause of the rule above, not a
62	  situation of its own. Split when a reader could arrive at the second rule without the first.
63	- **Separating the blocks** — one blank line between rules. The block is what a reader lands on,
64	  and an unbroken run of bullets makes them scan lines instead; the separation costs one token.
65	- **Ordering a file of many rules** — past roughly fifteen, group them under headings naming the
66	  surface each concerns, so a reader scans headings before subjects. A flat list that long makes
67	  every bold subject do the work one heading would.
68	- **Grouping that separates two rules which qualify each other** — add an explicit pointer from
69	  the general rule to its exception, or the general one reads as unconditional. That pointer is
70	  the one sentence a rewrite may add that its source didn't have; name it as an addition when
71	  you report the change.
72	- **Ordering the clauses** — the default first, then the `if you can't` fallback, then
73	  `consider` for an optional aid, then the `don't` that the earlier clauses make unnecessary.
74	- **Choosing modality** — grade it per clause and claim no more than the rule needs. Keep
75	  `never` and `always` for the genuinely absolute and reach for `prefer`, `avoid` or `rather
76	  than` otherwise; escalating a `don't` into a `never` changes the rule rather than rewording
77	  it.
78	- **Naming a mechanism** — name the check, helper or skill that owns the mechanics, and stop.
79	  Its parameters, options and failure modes live with it, and restating them here is a copy
80	  that goes stale. The exception is a mechanism you are telling the reader to *run*, below.
81	- **Telling the reader to *run* something** — ship the literal invocation in a fenced block, not
82	  the file's name. The reader is composing a call rather than looking a mechanism up, so a bare
83	  filename buys a probe every time — the `--help` that prints nothing, then the `cat`, then a
84	  hand-built command. (1)
85	- **Closing a block** — say what the other clauses make unnecessary ("don't also comment the
86	  duplication — the guard covers it"), so nobody adds belt-and-braces.
87	- **Keeping an exception** — an exception that changes what the reader would do is part of the
88	  rule; one that only reassures is padding.
89	- **Cutting a rule's prose** — drop rationale that only restates the rule, examples that
90	  re-express it, and mechanics another document owns. Keep the motivation itself: a consequence
91	  the reader needs in order to apply the rule under pressure earns its clause; rationale the
92	  reader doesn't need at act time goes to the references doc below.
93	- **Auditing a file of rules that already exists** — take each rule and ask what a reader would
94	  get wrong without it. Fold the one whose subject points back at its neighbour; cut the one another
95	  pack already carries, the one a check now enforces (keeping only the half the check can't see),
96	  and the one whose mechanism has since been retired — a rule naming code that no longer exists
97	  teaches a world the reader won't find.
98	- **Rewriting an existing rule** — carry the source's own strength forward. A rewrite must not
99	  weaken a rule, and it must not strengthen one either.
100	
101	## The references doc — where a rule's rationale lives
102	
103	A pack keeps **one** `references.md` beside its `RULES.md`, servicing all of the pack's prose
104	files and its checks. It exists for maintenance and review — the periodic pass that asks
105	whether a rule still earns its place needs the reason it was written — never for daily agentic
106	work: no rule sends its reader there, and no session loads it. So it stays in the repo that
107	owns the pack and never vendors: a member mounting a canon pack receives the rules, not the
108	reasoning behind them, and the pass that reaffirms them runs where the pack lives.
109	
110	- **Adding a rule that has a rationale** — write the brief rule in `RULES.md` (or the skill),
111	  and put the reason in `references.md`. End the rule with the bare marker — `… never a
112	  filesystem walk. (3)` — and nothing else: don't name the references file, don't link it,
113	  don't ask the reader to follow anything. Not every rule needs one; a rule whose reason is
114	  self-evident from its consequence clause carries no marker.
115	- **Writing the entry** — one bullet per entry, keyed by the citing file's own namespace:
116	  `- **(RULES-3)** <reason>` for a rule in `RULES.md`, `- **(<skill-name>-3)** <reason>` for a
117	  line in that skill's `SKILL.md`; the marker in the prose file stays the bare `(3)` and
118	  resolves within its own file's namespace. Write the reason so a future review can **reaffirm
119	  the rule from it**: what would have to be true for the rule to be retired.
120	  - A **workaround** explains the issue with not using it, with the evidence (the failing run,
121	    the error, the measured cost).
122	  - A **technology guideline** cites the original documentation it derives from.
123	  - An **owner decision** carries the language of the request that set it.
124	- **Numbering** — numbers are stable identifiers, not positions: the next entry takes its
125	  file's next unused number, a removed entry leaves a gap, and nothing ever renumbers (a
126	  renumber breaks every marker at once). One entry may serve several rules in its file; a rule
127	  may cite several entries (`(3, 7)`).
128	- **A check's rationale** — the entry points at the check, since a declaration admits no
129	  comment and no new key: `- **(check:growth-write-scope)** <reason>`, same reaffirmation
130	  standard. There is no marker on the check side.
131	- **Removing a rule or check** — remove its entry in the same change, unless another rule
132	  still cites it.
133	
134	The `references-integrity` check holds the mechanism together: every marker must resolve to an
135	entry in the pack's own `references.md`, and every `check:` entry must name a check the pack
136	still carries. The `rule-revalidation` task is the mechanism's consumer — it reaffirms
137	referenced rules and checks against their recorded reasons on its weekly pass.
138	
139	## Migrating an existing pack onto the references doc
140	
141	An existing pack — a repo's local pack, or a shared canon pack worked on canon-side (a member
142	never edits the mounted canon) — migrates opportunistically, one pack per pass, whenever a pass
143	is already editing it. An unmarked rule stays valid forever, so there is no fleet sweep to
144	force and no straggler to chase; the check only judges markers that exist.
145	
146	1. **Create `references.md`** beside the pack's `RULES.md` on its first entry, not before.
147	2. **Work each rule**: keep the act-time consequence clause inline; move review-only rationale —
148	   the evidence story, inline issue ids, a cost the reader doesn't need mid-act — into an entry
149	   and end the rule with its marker. Shrink-only on the rules side: a rule may lose review-only
150	   rationale in this pass, never gain text.
151	3. **Recover the missing reasons from history, source-first**: for a rule that states no reason,
152	   read the commit that added it and that commit's PR and issue *before* re-reading the rule —
